f6945bdfb38b: September 1 — "Not an Organization." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Akron, 1937. Eighteen alcoholics sat in a li
1db14edc90be: Akron, 1937. Eighteen alcoholics sat in a living room while Bill W. made his case: A.A. should hire paid missionaries, build a chain of hospitals that turned a profit, and publish a book. The room pushed back hard. Then it voted, and Bill won — "by the barest majority, and over the most strenuous objections," in his own account of it (A.A. Comes of Age). A.A. had just decided, democratically and in good faith, to turn itself into an organization. Nobody in that room was cynical about it. They believed structure would reach dying men faster, and they may well have been right. It never happened. Bill went east to raise the money and came back with nothing. Two years later the Big Book went to print, and page xiii carried the first thing A.A. ever said about itself in public: "We are not an organization in the conventional sense of the word." That sentence survived because a fundraising trip failed. It's also why the meeting you sat in this week has no owner, no dues, no membership committee, and nobody with the standing to put you out.

7571dc31c4d2: September 10 — "The Missing Clause." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. The whole safeguard in Tradition 9 is six wo
662132bfc07e: The whole safeguard in Tradition 9 is six words, and they are the six that get left out. The short form (Big Book, p. 562): "A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve." Service boards and committees are the offices that answer the phone, print the schedules and keep the lights on. Quote the Tradition without the ending and you have a permission slip — A.A. allows offices. Quote it whole and you have a leash: any body doing A.A.'s work answers downward, to the people it serves, or it is not doing A.A.'s work. That is the cheapest capture there is. Nobody has to lie. A sentence stops early, gets repeated, and starts to sound complete. So when a board, an office, a committee, or a program tells you it is part of A.A., ask the six-word question: who do you answer to? An A.A. service body answers to the groups, and the groups can stop paying for it tomorrow. A body that answers to owners, funders, or a head office is organized in exactly the way this Tradition says A.A. never will be. Read the Tradition to the end. The end is the point.
ff04ed07a86c: The safeguard is six words most people stop before. What have I accepted as settled because I only heard the first half?

483fc9080ec5: Nobody stands at the door of an A.A. meeting deciding who gets in. That was settled by the drunks who tried it. Early Cleveland had men posted for exactly that job — other members called them the "snifters," which an early member explained were "men who stood by the door, sniffing each man who came in" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers). Sniffing for liquor. Behind them stood the rules: you had to be hospitalized first, or visited by ten members, or passed by a committee. Then a man walked in with a couple of drinks in him. The snifters moved to throw him out, and somebody said: "Let him stay. Maybe something will seep in." He stayed. He got sober, "just as sober as the fellow who had been hospitalized or visited by ten members, there went another rule. In the end, pioneer A.A.'s broke so many of their own rules that there were no rules left!" That is where the open door came from. So when a programme puts an assessment, an intake, or a sign-off between you and a chair, understand what it is: the snifters, back at the door. The alcoholic still drinking is the whole reason the room exists. A.A. learned not to make him qualify for it.
fff44821c437: A.A. broke its own rules until none were left, because the drunk at the door was the point. Would I have got in the night I came?

907b0bbbbb01: Nobody runs an A.A. group for life. The Long Form says how it is done in one short sentence (Big Book, p. 565): "Rotating leadership is the best." The drunks in Cleveland worked that out before anyone wrote it down. In October 1939 they formed A.A.'s first central committee — seven people — and built the exit into it from day one: "one man and one woman dropped off each month to be replaced by the next in line according to seniority" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers) — seniority meaning time in A.A., not rank. Bill W. admitted what everyone had assumed until then: "Up to that time, all of our affairs had been in charge of the ultra-oldtimers, and we naturally supposed it would always be that way." Naturally supposed. That is how a person becomes a position — not by a vote, but by nobody thinking to ask. Rotation is the ask, built in, so the job always comes open and never turns into a man. It is also why the chair will be open to you. Now look at any room where the same person has run "the A.A. meeting" for years and is paid to. Nobody is rotating out of a salary. That room has a manager, and A.A. groups do not.
2aa1502147a2: A.A. built the exit into its first committee so no job could become a person. When did the chair in my meeting last change hands?
85f4444a2bf2: Grounded in: Big Book, long form, Tradition 9 (p. 565); Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers.

7f00fc5ffeac: The moment a group owns a treatment operation, the newcomer becomes the least urgent thing in the room. A.A. has the case on record (P-43, The Twelve Traditions Illustrated): in the early days some members thought "A.A. should cover the whole alcoholism field," and one group "built an all-purpose center, including a section for drying-out treatment" — a building of its own, with beds. The centre failed. The lesson did not. The same page gives the standing practice: "keep the operation of the facility completely separate from that of any A.A. group," and keep the A.A. name, and terms like Twelfth Step, out of the facility's name. Read that against today's storefronts. A business with "12 Step" on the sign and beds down the hall is the all-purpose centre, rebuilt. The newcomer is still being told to wait a minute.

a301c0e1ee76: The heart of A.A. cannot be organized, and anyone offering to organize it is selling something else. c36bccc52125: September 15 — "Responsibility, Not Authority." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Every service job in A.A. looks l
51fa1ebec731: Every service job in A.A. looks like a position, and none of them are one. The pamphlet is exact about the difference (A.A. pamphlet P-43): "All the way from coffee-brewers to trustees on the General Service Board, those who take part in A.A. service work are assuming responsibility — not taking on authority." Then it lists who answers to whom, and the list runs one way only. "Group officers are responsible to the members of the group; intergroup committees, to the groups in one locality," and on up until "the General Service Office and Board and the board's committees, to all groups and members everywhere." Hold that against the way every other organisation you have dealt with is built. The same pamphlet does it for you: "In an average business corporation, the board has final power to determine company plans and policy." And then A.A.'s: "In industry, branch offices jump when the home office speaks. Our GSO is just a clearinghouse of A.A. information, offering suggestions based on experiences reported to it by groups." So the question to ask about anything doing A.A.'s work is not what it is called, or who runs it, or whether they mean well. It is which way the sentences run. A body that reports to the people it serves is doing A.A. service. A body that instructs them has become something else, and it did not need to announce the change.
3a585e4cb697: Every job in A.A. is a responsibility somebody accepted, never an authority somebody was handed. Who does the person running my meeting answer to, and how would I find out?

0be118c16721: No committee decides who is fit for A.A. Oscar W. helped start a group, went back to visit, and found four ministers in the front row (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers). He was delighted — four ministers in A.A.! One of them stood up and set him straight: "We're not drunken ministers, We are the screening committee for Alcoholics Anonymous, to determine who is fit for membership." Read the title again. Not friends of the group. A screening committee, ruling on fitness, in a fellowship whose only requirement is a desire to stop drinking. Nobody invaded that room. Somebody invited them, because they were respectable and seemed like the right people to have around. That is how it happens — not by force, by help. The Long Form leaves no gap for it (Big Book, p. 563): "we may refuse none who wish to recover." None. Not by a minister, a clinician, or an intake form. So when a building tells you it will "assess" whether you are ready for A.A., you are looking at four ministers in a front row. A.A. has no screening committee. It never accepted one.

30e64a02186d: September 17 — "A Legal Bludgeon." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. A.A. was offered the power to govern, by law,
636e57354ddb: A.A. was offered the power to govern, by law, and turned it down. After a film studio misused the A.A. name, the board's own chairman — a lawyer — proposed a Congressional Charter, an act of Congress protecting the name the way the Red Cross is protected. Bill W. was honest about what headquarters saw in it (A.A. Comes of Age): "a legal bludgeon of this size and weight could easily be used" on anyone who still defied the law. "It looked like a grand idea and we at the Headquarters were all for it." The delegates — the members the groups had sent — said no. Their reasoning is the plainest sentence in this month: "It would mean the legal organization of a fellowship whose Traditions insisted on its being unorganized." Their written finding went further: "A Congressional incorporation would create by law a power to govern which would be contrary to, and violative of, our Traditions." A power to govern. That is what A.A. refused, even to protect its own name from people misusing it. So hold that against anyone today who wants to hold the name, license the meetings, or certify who may carry the message "to protect A.A." A.A. already decided what protection costs. It chose the open door and no bludgeon.
045b39420bf6: A.A. refused a law protecting its own name because the protection came with a power to govern. What protection have I wanted that would have cost more than the thing it protected?

44185026441b: The people this Tradition guards against are not history. A.A.'s own pamphlet says so in the present tense (P-43, The Twelve Traditions Illustrated): "And they're still around — the members who are always sure that they're always right — the members who are happily ready to assume all the burdens of leadership and grimly unwilling to share them, let alone give them up." f700f7d134a8: December 1937. Bill sat in John D. Rockefeller Jr.'s board room and asked for money to build something specific: a chain of hospitals where alcoholics would be treated, staffed by A.A. members, paid for out of the proceeds. Albert Scott, who chaired the trustees of Riverside Church, asked the question that ended it (A.A. Comes of Age): "Won't money spoil this thing?" Rockefeller sent a man to Akron to look, got back a recommendation for fifty thousand dollars, read it, and said no. "I think money will spoil this." Be clear about what A.A. almost became. Not a fellowship that referred people to hospitals — a fellowship that owned them. Beds, staff, fees, admissions, discharges. And whoever owns the building has to govern it: decide who gets in, who pays, and who is asked to leave. That is an organization, and Tradition 9 is the sentence saying A.A. can never be one. Tradition 9 asks one thing of any body doing A.A.'s work: is it "directly responsible to those they serve" (Big Book, p. 562)? Nine years after that board room, A.A. wrote the answer down, so it would never again depend on a rich man saying no.

9dedf930bb13: The Absence of a Boss Is Not a Vacancy

When a programme says it will organize A.A. for its clients, the absence of a boss is not a vacancy. It is the design.

ead34df00c9e: September 21 — "A Great Many Sheets of Paper." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Every rule was reasonable. Added t
b4d8ab2359d7: A Great Many Sheets of Paper
4137c998b716: Every rule was reasonable. Added together they would have kept nine out of ten of A.A.'s own founders out. Around 1943 the head office asked every group to send in its membership rules. Listing them, Bill recalled, "took a great many sheets of paper" (Pass It On). Then he did the arithmetic: "If all these edicts had been in force everywhere at once, it would have been practically impossible for any alcoholic to have ever joined A.A. About nine-tenths of our oldest and best members could never have got by!" Nine-tenths. Including the men who wrote the rules. No group had done anything cruel. Each had added one requirement, for one good reason, after one bad night — and no one could see the total until somebody stacked the sheets. That survey is the closest thing A.A. has to a photograph of what organizing a fellowship does to the person it exists for. 24f8f6b16af6: In A.A., a title carries no power. None. The Long Form of Tradition 9 (Big Book, p. 565) says it in one line: "true leaders in A.A. are but trusted and experienced servants of the whole. They derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern." Secretary, chair, treasurer, trustee — each is a job somebody took on so the coffee gets made, the rent gets paid and the office stays open, and each one rotates. Nobody holds a rank. Nobody can tell you what to do. The Big Book states the founding decision the same way (p. xix): "our leaders might serve but never govern." So look hard at the titles that come with today's meetings. Facilitator. Coordinator. Program director. Clinical lead. Those are real jobs in the buildings that pay for them, and inside an A.A. group they mean nothing. If the person at the front of the room has authority over you — can require you to attend, can remove you, can sign off on your progress — that room is being governed, and A.A. groups are not governed. Whatever it is, it is not the thing this Tradition describes.
3e8979f9bcca: No title in A.A. carries authority; everyone at the front is a servant who rotates out. Whose title have I mistaken for the right to run me?

7a4ac019382e: A meeting a facility can cancel is a meeting that facility governs, and an A.A. group is governed by nobody. The Long Form is exact about where treatment belongs (Big Book, p. 564): "hospitals, as well as other places of recuperation, ought to be well outside A.A.—and medically supervised." Places of recuperation — where people go to dry out — outside. Not partnered, not hosting, not in-house. The same page closes the door on the arrangement itself: "An A.A. group can bind itself to no one." And Tradition 3 sets the one condition on being a group at all — two or three alcoholics may call themselves an A.A. group "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation" (p. 563). Now look at the meeting on a treatment schedule. The facility picks the time, picks the room, staffs the chair, fills the seats with its clients, and can strike it from the calendar. That meeting is affiliated — tied to the facility — bound, and governed. Call it the facility's meeting. It is not an A.A. group, and nobody who runs it can tell you what A.A. requires of you, because A.A. requires nothing. The real thing is a room where the people in the chairs are the only ones who can close it.
55a28b0cac9e: Whoever can cancel the meeting governs it. Who can cancel mine?
